clue.text: Opening vacation

definitions.meaning: first meaning: an alcove or hollow set back into a wall
second meaning: a break when parliament or the courts stop sitting

explanation.walkthrough: Two words side by side read like the start of a holiday, but each separately defines the same word.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both a niche or alcove in a wall and a formal break from business, as in a parliamentary holiday.

clue.text: Devil in Lucifer as callous

indicators.note: the answer sits inside the run of letters that follows, spanning word breaks

parts.note: the letters run across the end of the first word, the whole second word and the start of the third

explanation.surface: A description of Satan as a heartless figure.
explanation.walkthrough: Lucifer pulls toward the definition, since he is the Devil, but he only houses the letters; 'Devil' itself is the definition, in the playful sense of a little devil.
explanation.definitionFit: Calling a mischievous child 'a little devil' is the same affectionate reproach as calling them a rogue or scamp.

clue.text: Reoccurrence of tea dance

indicators.note: something that recurs again and again appears several times over, so one word is laid down repeatedly in a row

parts.note: cha is an old British slang word for tea, from Chinese
the same word again, as the recurrence demands
and a third time

explanation.surface: A tea dance being held once more.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tea dance' looks like one phrase, a genteel afternoon dance; split it, and the drink word is used three times before the dance it names.
explanation.definitionFit: The cha-cha-cha is a Latin American ballroom dance of Cuban origin with a quick triple step.

clue.text: Weasel, meadow animal?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a sly, treacherous person
second meaning, taken literally: a serpent lying among the meadow's turf

explanation.walkthrough: Weasel looks like the name of a field creature, but it is the figurative sense of a sneaky person; the question mark flags the literal reading of the idiom.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom names a hidden traitor, while read word for word it describes a reptile lurking in a field.

clue.text: Originally puny thing, little matter?

indicators.note: originally means at the start, so only the opening letter of the next word is kept

parts.note: the initial letter of puny
an article is an item or object

explanation.surface: Something tiny and insignificant, of no great importance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Little matter' reads as 'unimportant', but the question mark signals a physics sense: a tiny bit of matter.
explanation.definitionFit: A particle is a minute fragment of physical substance, so it is literally a small piece of matter.

clue.text: A barrier, one of two in garden?

parts.note: taken as written
a dam is a wall holding back water

explanation.surface: A fence or wall, one of a pair in someone's garden.
explanation.walkthrough: The garden is Eden, and the two in it are the first man and woman of Genesis.
explanation.definitionFit: In the Bible story the first man lived in the Garden of Eden with Eve, making him half of its pair of human residents.

clue.text: What to do with false beard? Don't complain!

definitions.text: What to do with false beard?
definitions.meaning: first meaning, taken literally: a fake beard is put on and worn on the jaw
second meaning: accept a setback stoically

explanation.surface: Someone told to stop moaning about wearing a fake beard in a costume.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark marks the literal, jokey reading of an idiom whose real sense is the instruction after it.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means accepting a blow or misfortune bravely without grumbling, as a boxer absorbs a punch.

clue.text: Get on top of Chopin with musical refrain

indicators.note: the top of a down word is its first letter, so just that letter is taken

parts.note: the opening letter of the composer's name
a lick is a short repeated phrase played by a musician

explanation.surface: Mastering a Chopin piece with a recurring tune.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Get on top of' reads as mastering, but the definition is only 'Get on', in the sense of two people getting along.
explanation.definitionFit: When two people get on, they hit it off; to click is the informal idiom for that instant rapport.

clue.text: Not all attending, cancel event held for Armistice Day, say?

indicators.note: if not everyone turns up, only part of the group is present, so only some of the letters are used
what is held is contained, so the answer is kept within the words

parts.note: the letters span the end of the first word, all of the second and the start of the third

explanation.surface: A poorly attended commemoration being called off.
explanation.walkthrough: Armistice Day falls on 11 November, marking the 1918 ceasefire at the eleventh hour of the eleventh day of the eleventh month; 'say' signals an example.
explanation.definitionFit: Armistice Day is an example of a date that is the eleventh, since it falls on that day of November.

clue.text: Fraud, an unorthodox priest?

parts.note: a sham is a fake or deception
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone denouncing a cleric with odd beliefs as a fake.
explanation.walkthrough: The comma makes 'Fraud' look like the verdict on the priest; it is simply the first piece.
explanation.definitionFit: A shaman is a spiritual healer in tribal religions, a priestly figure outside any orthodox church.

clue.text: Champion with team — cheeky thing?

parts.note: to champion a cause is to support or back it
a side is a sports team

explanation.surface: A winner and their team behaving impudently.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Champion' looks like a noun, a title-holder, but it works as the verb meaning support.
explanation.definitionFit: The buttocks are informally called cheeks, so the bottom is jokingly a thing made of cheeks.

clue.text: Massive test locking up first of offenders for racism?

indicators.note: to lock someone up is to shut them inside, so one piece encloses another

parts.note: massive means very large
to try is to test or attempt

indicators.note: the first of a word is its opening letter, which alone is kept

parts.note: the opening letter of offenders

explanation.surface: A major trial imprisoning a racist offender.
explanation.walkthrough: Offenders and locking up suggest a courtroom, but they are just a letter source and its placement.
explanation.definitionFit: Racism is one example of prejudiced intolerance toward a group, hence the question mark marking it as an instance.

clue.text: Strapping top of leg, that ice scattered around it

indicators.note: to lie around something is to surround it, so the letter just mentioned goes inside
things scattered are thrown about into a new disorder, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, ready to be rearranged

indicators.note: the top of a word is its first letter, which alone is kept

parts.note: the opening letter of leg

explanation.surface: Bandaging a thigh with ice strewn about it after an injury.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Strapping' tempts as the sports bandage of the surface; it is the definition, meaning burly. 'It' points back to the leg letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A strapping person is big and muscular, the same physique described by a word for a sporty, fit build.

clue.text: Relish tricky situation

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a sharp condiment of preserved vegetables
second meaning: a predicament or awkward fix

explanation.walkthrough: 'Relish' reads as a verb, to enjoy a difficulty, but it is the noun for a condiment.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names both a vinegary preserve served with food and, idiomatically, a mess someone has got into.

clue.text: As toast may be without starter, it's said

indicators.note: a starter is the first course, and going without it means the opening letter is dropped

parts.note: toast is often spread with butter

explanation.surface: Toast eaten without a first course, as someone remarks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Starter' suggests a meal around the toast, but it means the first letter is lost.
explanation.definitionFit: To utter something is to speak it aloud, so words uttered are words spoken, the same past participle sense.

clue.text: Remarkable twister is in Toronto after winding through Connecticut!

indicators.note: to pass through something is to run inside it, so the rearranged letters sit within the abbreviation

parts.note: CT is the postal abbreviation of the US state

indicators.note: a winding course twists and turns, so the letters are bent into a new order

parts.note: taken as written, ready to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A tornado tearing from Connecticut up to Toronto.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Twister' looks like a tornado, matching the storm track in the surface, but it is a person who twists.
explanation.definitionFit: A contortionist is a performer who bends the body into extraordinary shapes, an impressive human twister.

clue.text: Funny one-liners in part of Oxford, say

indicators.note: something funny is odd or peculiar, so the letters are put into an odd order

parts.note: taken as written, without the hyphen

explanation.surface: Jokes cracked at a college of Oxford University.
explanation.walkthrough: Oxford looks like the university city, but an oxford is also a laced leather shoe; 'say' marks it as an example.
explanation.definitionFit: The cushioned lining inside a shoe is one component of an oxford, a classic lace-up shoe style.

clue.text: Hellcat transported by boy set off

indicators.note: something transported is carried inside a vehicle, so one piece rides within another

parts.note: a son is a male child
a hellcat is a spiteful, fierce woman, like a witch

explanation.surface: A boy carrying off a vicious woman, who then leaves.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Set off' reads as departing, but it means starting a device, as when an alarm is set off.
explanation.definitionFit: To set off a machine or alarm is to activate it, the same as turning it on with a control.

clue.text: Battered by storms, bedraggled plant demolished, primula ultimately saved

parts.words: Battered by storms, bedraggled plant demolished, primula ultimately saved
parts.note: surface reading: a gardener surveying storm damage, one flower pulling through
setter's reading: one plant was flattened while the primula came through the bad spell, the two halves of the phrase

explanation.surface: A garden after a gale: one plant flattened, the primula just surviving.
explanation.walkthrough: The scene acts out the compound: one plant was beaten, and the primula weathered the storm, meaning it survived.
explanation.definitionFit: Something weather-beaten has been worn and damaged by exposure to wind, rain and storms.

clue.text: Loud insect circling wood

indicators.note: to circle something is to go all the way round it, so one piece surrounds another

parts.note: a fly is a common insect
ash is a tree and its timber

explanation.surface: A noisy bug buzzing round a copse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Loud' suggests noise from the buzzing insect, but here it describes garish colours or clothes.
explanation.definitionFit: Loud clothes are showy and gaudy; the word for ostentatiously eye-catching style is a synonym in that visual sense.

clue.text: Caribbean island, terribly captivating land

indicators.note: to captivate is literally to take captive, so one piece holds another prisoner inside it

parts.note: Togo is a country in West Africa
taken as a clipped form of bad, a word for terrible, with its last letter cut

explanation.surface: An island in the West Indies that is enormously charming.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Terribly captivating' reads as 'very charming'; split up, 'land' is the African country and 'terribly' supplies a short letter pair, a loose clipping.
explanation.definitionFit: Tobago is the smaller partner island of Trinidad in the southern Caribbean, forming one nation with it.

clue.text: Times getting stick, crikey!

parts.note: times as in multiplied by, as in three by four
to gum something is to stick it down with glue

explanation.surface: A shocked reaction to The Times newspaper being criticised.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Times' tempts as the newspaper being given stick, meaning criticism; it is the multiplication word. By gum is a mild northern English oath.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are mild exclamations of surprise; the northern English oath is a minced form of 'by God'.

clue.text: Intellectual emptying beer into breakfast!

indicators.note: putting one thing into another places it inside, so one piece goes within the other

parts.note: cereal is a typical breakfast food

indicators.note: emptying something removes its contents, leaving only its outer shell of letters

parts.note: just the first and last letters of beer

explanation.surface: A brainy type pouring beer onto their morning cornflakes.
explanation.walkthrough: The exclamation mark plays up the absurd picture of beer on breakfast; 'Intellectual' is the definition, an adjective here.
explanation.definitionFit: Cerebral means relating to the brain, and so describes a person or work that is highly intellectual rather than emotional.

clue.text: Small ship for small island

parts.note: S is the standard abbreviation for small, as on clothing labels
an ark is a ship, as in Noah's

explanation.surface: A little boat bought for a tiny island.
explanation.walkthrough: Sark is one of the Channel Islands, between England and France, famous for banning cars.
explanation.definitionFit: Sark is a tiny Channel Island of about two square miles, so 'small island' fits it exactly.

clue.text: Swine leads huge crowd, hosting a winter celebration

indicators.note: whatever leads goes in front, so this piece is placed before the rest

parts.note: a hog is a pig

indicators.note: a host has guests inside their home, so one piece takes in another

parts.note: the many is a great number of people
taken as written

explanation.surface: A pig at the head of a big crowd throwing a midwinter party.
explanation.walkthrough: Hogmanay is the Scottish name for New Year's Eve and its festivities.
explanation.definitionFit: Hogmanay is the Scots New Year's Eve festival held on 31 December, a celebration in the depths of winter.

clue.text: Reduced work in new show — oh dear

indicators.note: one piece placed in another sits inside it
making something new means remaking it, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, ready to be rearranged
opus, a musical work, cut short to its usual abbreviation

explanation.surface: A disappointing, scaled-down production in a fresh show.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Reduced work' sounds like cuts to a theatre production; it means the abbreviation of opus, as in Op. 9 on a concert programme.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are mild exclamations said after a small mistake or mishap, so either can stand in for the other.

clue.text: Similar title makes an odd headline in the end

indicators.note: something odd is strange or out of order, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, ready to be rearranged

indicators.note: the end of a word is its final letter, which alone is kept

parts.note: the final letter of headline

explanation.surface: A newspaper editor finds a matching heading produces an awkward headline.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Makes' looks like a link verb, but it belongs to the fodder; only 'headline' is trimmed to its last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A namesake is a person or thing bearing the same name as another, so it shares a matching label.

clue.text: One in seven affected by hay fever?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: one of the Seven Dwarfs in the Snow White story
second meaning: inclined to keep sneezing, as an allergy sufferer is

explanation.surface: A statistic about how many people suffer from pollen allergy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One in seven' reads like a prevalence figure for hay fever, but the seven are Snow White's dwarfs.
explanation.definitionFit: Disney's dwarf is named for constant sneezing, and an allergy sufferer in pollen season is literally prone to sneezes.
